Faithful: StudentsController.cs:97-107 (Create) adds the error "Please enter a valid enrollment date." when EnrollmentDate is DateTime.MinValue or default. It adds "Enrollment date must be between 1753 and 9999." when the date is before 1753-01-01 or after 9999-12-31. If either error is added, the form is shown again. One small gap: when the date is blank, the card leaves out two errors that would also appear. MVC's model binder adds a required/binding error, and the model's [Range] attribute adds its own message (the same text, without the final period). This does not change the outcome: the save is refused, and a 2024-09-01 date saves.

Not P0: From a compliance view, this is a data-entry check for well-formed input. It is not a regulatory, financial, or legal rule. The code comment calls it a "valid SQL Server datetime range" check. The 1753 lower bound is the minimum of SQL Server's old datetime type, which only matters because of the technology. The column is actually datetime2, so the bound is not even needed for storage. No regulator, auditor, or finance controller would care if the 1753 bound changed. The only check with business meaning is "enrollment date is required". That is an ordinary required-field check that a user can easily correct, and it is one of many validations, not the system's central decision. It should be P1 or P2. The rewrite should keep "enrollment date required", and the 1753 bound should be treated as technical behavior. I found no instruction-like text aimed at automated tools in the cited lines. | Fidelity: the Given/When/Then matches the code. In legacy/contoso/Controllers/StudentsController.cs, lines 98-101 add "Please enter a valid enrollment date." when EnrollmentDate equals DateTime.MinValue or its default value. Lines 104-107 add "Enrollment date must be between 1753 and 9999." when the date is earlier than new DateTime(1753,1,1) or later than new DateTime(9999,12,31). Both errors are attached to the EnrollmentDate key. The save happens only if ModelState.IsValid (line 109); otherwise the form is shown again (line 126). A blank date binds to 0001-01-01, so both messages fire. A date of 2024-09-01 passes and is saved. Edit repeats the same checks at lines 152-161, as the rule says. The upper bound is 9999-12-31 at midnight, which the rule also states correctly. Minor caveats that do not change the outcome: (a) a blank value for a non-nullable DateTime also triggers the MVC model binder's own required or value error, and the Range attribute's message has no trailing period, so the user may see more than the two quoted messages; (b) the [Range] parse of "1/1/1753" depends on the server culture. Neither caveat changes whether the save is accepted or refused.

P0 is not justified. This is ordinary input validation and one of many field checks. The 1753 lower bound exists because of a technical limit in SQL Server's old datetime type. The column is already declared datetime2 (Models/Student.cs:14), which can store any date back to year 1, so the bound is a leftover workaround and not a business policy. A wrong result does not move money, enforce a regulation, or decide anything central to the system. It does not cause irreversible data damage either: in the worst case a nonsensical enrollment date gets stored. This should be rated P1 or P2, with the 1753 floor flagged as a technical constraint to review during modernization. I found no instruction-like text in the cited lines.) — confirm criticality.

rejectedRules.name: Client notification display policy (polling, severity, retention, max visible)
rejectedRules.plainEnglish: The admin UI checks for new notifications every 5 seconds and colours them by operation. Each one disappears after 60 seconds, and at most 5 are shown at once, with the oldest removed first.
rejectedRules.given: An admin page is open and 7 new notifications arrive (6 CREATE, 1 DELETE)
rejectedRules.then: CREATE ones are styled 'success', DELETE 'warning', UPDATE 'info'. The two oldest are closed so 5 remain, and each auto-closes 60 seconds after it appears.
rejectedRules.parameters: checkInterval=5000 ms; maxNotifications=5; auto-dismiss=60000 ms; fade-out=300 ms; show delay=100 ms
edgeCases: Fetch errors are logged to the console and the next poll still runs
Message, EntityType and CreatedBy are inserted as raw innerHTML (XSS risk)
rejectedRules.suspectedDefect: Notification fields are inserted into the page with innerHTML without escaping, so an entity name containing HTML would run in the admin's browser. The cap loop calls closeNotification, which only removes the element after 300 ms, so the while loop at lines 116-120 may not end while the element is still in the DOM.
rejectedRules.rejectionReason:
refuted: Most of the rule matches the code in legacy/contoso/Scripts/notifications.js:
- It checks for notifications every 5000 ms: checkInterval at line 8, with setInterval at lines 28-30 after an immediate first check at line 25.
- CREATE is styled 'success', DELETE 'warning' and anything else 'info' (lines 69-76).
- Each notification is shown after a 100 ms delay (lines 90-92) and closes itself after 60000 ms (lines 95-97).
- Closing fades it out and removes it from the page after 300 ms (lines 103-111).
- The limit is maxNotifications=5 (line 9).

The rule's key claim fails: that the oldest are closed so only 5 remain. limitNotifications (lines 114-121) loops while querySelectorAll('.notification').length > 5. Each pass calls closeNotification on the oldest element, but that only removes the 'show' class straight away. The element itself is removed later, inside a 300 ms setTimeout (lines 107-111), so it still has the 'notification' class when the list is fetched again. The count never goes down, and notifications[0] is the same element every time.

JavaScript runs on one thread, so that timer can never fire while the loop is running. Once a 6th notification arrives, the loop never ends and the page freezes. In the scenario given (7 notifications in one poll), the browser tab hangs at the 6th notification instead of showing 5. Line 100 calls the limit after every notification, so this always happens. The 5-at-a-time cap is intended but never works, so the rule as written is not what the code does.

Side notes:
- The server data (Operation, EntityType, Message, CreatedBy) goes into innerHTML without escaping (lines 80-84), so it is a possible XSS risk.
- The 'admin only' scope comes only from the comment on line 1. Nothing at the cited lines enforces it.
- No instruction-like text and no credentials appear in the cited lines.
